::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain why least squares becomes **unstable** with many or correlated predictors, and how a **penalty** trades bias for variance;
- describe **ridge**, **lasso** and **elastic net** and the role of the two tuning parameters $\lambda$ and $\alpha$;
- prepare a design matrix correctly and fit penalized models with **glmnet**, reading **coefficient paths** and **cross-validation curves**;
- choose $\lambda$ with `cv.glmnet()` and explain why **`lambda.1se`** gives a simpler, more stable model than `lambda.min`;
- compare penalized models with OLS by **repeated cross-validation**, and tune an elastic net with **tidymodels**.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(glmnet)
library(tidymodels)   # rsample, recipes, parsnip, workflows, tune,
                      # yardstick, dials + dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, tibble
```
:::


## 1. Why penalize?

In [Model selection](40-model-selection.qmd) we saw that adding predictors always improves the fit to the data at hand, but can make predictions for new data worse, and that choosing predictors with `step()` is unstable. Let us look at the problem from another angle.

`mtcars` has 32 cars and 10 candidate predictors of fuel consumption (`mpg`). We treat `cyl`, `vs` and `am` as categorical:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cars <- mtcars |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl),
         vs = factor(vs),
         am = factor(am, labels = c("auto", "manual")))

m_ols <- lm(mpg ~ ., data = cars)
summary(m_ols)$r.squared
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.8816
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(m_ols)$coefficients |> round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)   17.820     16.306   1.093    0.287
#> cyl6          -1.660      2.262  -0.734    0.472
#> cyl8           1.637      4.316   0.379    0.708
#> disp           0.014      0.017   0.799    0.433
#> hp            -0.046      0.027  -1.701    0.104
#> drat           0.026      1.676   0.016    0.988
#> wt            -3.806      1.847  -2.061    0.053
#> qsec           0.647      0.722   0.896    0.381
#> vs1            1.747      2.273   0.769    0.451
#> ammanual       2.617      2.005   1.306    0.207
#> gear           0.764      1.457   0.525    0.606
#> carb           0.509      0.942   0.540    0.595
```


:::
:::


The model explains 88% of the variance in `mpg`, yet **not a single coefficient** is significant at the 5% level. The reason is that the predictors are strongly correlated:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cor(mtcars[, c("cyl", "disp", "hp", "wt")]) |> round(2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>       cyl disp   hp   wt
#> cyl  1.00 0.90 0.83 0.78
#> disp 0.90 1.00 0.79 0.89
#> hp   0.83 0.79 1.00 0.66
#> wt   0.78 0.89 0.66 1.00
```


:::
:::


Big engines (`disp`), many cylinders, high horsepower and heavy cars go together. With so much overlap, the data cannot tell which of them "really" matters, so the individual coefficients are very uncertain. We can see that uncertainty by refitting the model on **bootstrap** samples (see [The bootstrap](../07-probability/31-bootstrap.qmd)):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
boot_coef <- t(replicate(500, {
  rows <- sample(nrow(cars), replace = TRUE)
  coef(lm(mpg ~ ., data = cars[rows, ]))[c("wt", "disp", "hp")]
}))
colMeans(boot_coef > 0)   # share of bootstrap fits with a positive sign
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    wt  disp    hp 
#> 0.068 0.798 0.230
```


:::
:::


The coefficient of engine displacement is positive in 80% of the bootstrap fits and negative in the rest; even horsepower changes sign in 23% of them. Least squares is **unbiased** but has **high variance**: small changes in the data produce large changes in the estimates, and in the predictions that depend on them.

**Penalized regression** accepts a small amount of **bias** — it pulls ("shrinks") the coefficients towards zero — in exchange for a large reduction in **variance**. When predictors are many or correlated, this trade usually improves predictions on new data.

## 2. The bias–variance trade-off, by simulation

To see the trade in action, we simulate many datasets with two highly correlated predictors (correlation 0.95) and true coefficients $\beta_1 = \beta_2 = 1$. For each dataset we estimate $\beta_1$ by least squares and by **ridge regression**, which adds a penalty $\lambda$ on the size of the coefficients. Ridge has a closed-form solution that takes a few lines of code (details in the "Going deeper" box of Section 3):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ridge_coef <- function(X, y, lambda) {
  Xc <- scale(X, scale = FALSE)          # centre the predictors
  yc <- y - mean(y)
  n <- nrow(X)
  drop(solve(crossprod(Xc) / n + lambda * diag(ncol(X)),
             crossprod(Xc, yc) / n))
}
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
sims <- replicate(2000, {
  x1 <- rnorm(30)
  x2 <- 0.95 * x1 + sqrt(1 - 0.95^2) * rnorm(30)   # cor(x1, x2) = 0.95
  y <- 1 * x1 + 1 * x2 + rnorm(30, sd = 2)
  X <- cbind(x1, x2)
  c(OLS = ridge_coef(X, y, 0)[1], ridge = ridge_coef(X, y, 0.5)[1])
})
est <- tibble(method = rep(c("OLS", "ridge"), times = ncol(sims)),
              beta1 = as.vector(sims))
est |>
  summarise(mean = mean(beta1), sd = sd(beta1),
            mse = mean((beta1 - 1)^2), .by = method)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   method   mean     sd     mse
#>   <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 OLS    1.025  1.235  1.524  
#> 2 ridge  0.7867 0.1800 0.07791
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(est, aes(beta1, fill = method)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-3, 5)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[1]), y = "Number of datasets", fill = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Estimates of a coefficient whose true value is 1 (dashed line) in 2000 simulated datasets. OLS is centred on the truth but very spread out; ridge is slightly biased towards zero but far more precise.](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-bias-variance-1.png){#fig-bias-variance fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- **OLS** is unbiased (mean 1.02, close to 1) but its estimates have a standard deviation of 1.23: in many datasets it gets even the sign wrong.
- **Ridge** is biased (mean 0.79), but its standard deviation is only 0.18.
- The **mean squared error** (MSE = bias² + variance) is what matters for accuracy: 1.52 for OLS versus 0.08 for ridge. A little bias bought a large gain.
:::

Too much penalty, however, shrinks everything towards zero and the bias dominates (Exercise 6). The amount of penalty, $\lambda$, is a **tuning parameter** that we will choose by cross-validation.

## 3. Ridge, lasso and elastic net

All three methods minimise the usual residual sum of squares **plus a penalty** on the size of the coefficients. The **glmnet** package, which we use throughout, solves

$$
\min_{\beta_0,\,\beta}\;
\underbrace{\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta\big)^2}_{\text{fit}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\lambda\left[\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\,\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2 + \alpha\,\lVert\beta\rVert_1\right]}_{\text{penalty}},
$$

where $\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2 = \sum_j \beta_j^2$ (sum of squares) and $\lVert\beta\rVert_1 = \sum_j |\beta_j|$ (sum of absolute values). The intercept $\beta_0$ is **not** penalised.

| Method | $\alpha$ | Penalty | Typical behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ridge** | 0 | $\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_j \beta_j^2$ | shrinks all coefficients smoothly; none becomes exactly 0; shares weight among correlated predictors |
| **Lasso** | 1 | $\lambda \sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert$ | shrinks and sets some coefficients **exactly to 0**: variable selection |
| **Elastic net** | between 0 and 1 | a mix of both | selects variables, but keeps groups of correlated predictors together more than the lasso |

The two tuning parameters:

- $\lambda \ge 0$ sets the **strength** of the penalty. $\lambda = 0$ gives ordinary least squares; as $\lambda$ grows, coefficients shrink towards 0.
- $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ sets the **type** of penalty (ridge ↔ lasso).

**Lasso** stands for *least absolute shrinkage and selection operator*.

::: {.callout-important}
## Standardise the predictors

The penalty treats all coefficients alike, but the size of a coefficient depends on the **units** of its predictor: the coefficient of weight in tonnes is 1000 times that of weight in kilograms. Without standardisation, the penalty would depend on arbitrary unit choices. `glmnet()` therefore **standardises the predictors internally** (`standardize = TRUE`, the default) and reports the coefficients back on the **original** scale. In tidymodels we standardise explicitly with `step_normalize()` in a recipe (Section 10).
:::

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the geometry of ridge and lasso

The penalized problem is equivalent to minimising the RSS **subject to a budget** on the coefficients: $\sum_j \beta_j^2 \le s$ (ridge) or $\sum_j |\beta_j| \le s$ (lasso), where a smaller budget $s$ corresponds to a larger $\lambda$. With two coefficients, the ridge budget is a **disc** and the lasso budget a **diamond**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rss_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(b1 = seq(-1.5, 3, length.out = 200),
                               b2 = seq(-1.5, 3, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(rss = (b1 - 2)^2 + 1.2 * (b1 - 2) * (b2 - 1.2) + (b2 - 1.2)^2)
angle <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
circle <- tibble(b1 = cos(angle), b2 = sin(angle))
diamond <- tibble(b1 = c(1, 0, -1, 0, 1), b2 = c(0, 1, 0, -1, 0))

ggplot(rss_grid, aes(b1, b2)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = rss), bins = 12, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_path(data = circle, colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_path(data = diamond, colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = 2, y = 1.2, size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.15, y = 1.35, label = "OLS") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = expression(beta[1]), y = expression(beta[2]))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Contours of the residual sum of squares (ellipses, centred on the OLS estimate) and the ridge (circle) and lasso (diamond) constraint regions. The penalized solution is where the smallest ellipse touches the region. The diamond has corners on the axes, so the lasso solution often lands on one, where a coefficient is exactly zero.](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-geometry-1.png){#fig-geometry fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


The disc has no corners, so the ridge solution almost never has a coordinate exactly equal to 0; it simply moves towards the origin. The diamond's corners lie on the axes; the first contact with an ellipse frequently happens at a corner, which sets one coefficient to exactly zero. In many dimensions the $\ell_1$ ball has many corners and edges, which is why the lasso produces **sparse** solutions.

Two more facts:

- **Ridge** has the closed form $\hat\beta_\lambda = (X^\top X/n + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y/n$ for centred data (the function `ridge_coef()` above). Adding $\lambda I$ makes the matrix invertible even when predictors are collinear or $p > n$.
- **Lasso** has no closed form; glmnet uses **coordinate descent**, updating one coefficient at a time with a "soft-thresholding" step that sets small coefficients to 0. It computes the whole **path** of solutions for a decreasing sequence of $\lambda$ values very quickly, re-using each solution as the starting point for the next.
:::

## 4. Preparing the data for glmnet

`glmnet()` does not take a formula; it needs a numeric **matrix** `x` of predictors and a vector `y`. `model.matrix()` converts a data frame with factors into such a matrix, creating **dummy (indicator) variables** for each factor:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
X <- model.matrix(mpg ~ ., data = cars)[, -1]   # drop the intercept column
y <- cars$mpg
dim(X)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 32 11
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
colnames(X)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  [1] "cyl6"     "cyl8"     "disp"     "hp"       "drat"     "wt"      
#>  [7] "qsec"     "vs1"      "ammanual" "gear"     "carb"
```


:::
:::


Each factor with $k$ levels becomes $k - 1$ dummy columns: `cyl` gives `cyl6` and `cyl8`, with 4 cylinders as the reference level. We drop the column of ones (`[, -1]`) because glmnet fits its own (unpenalised) intercept.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A classic mistake: one dummy too many

A common recipe is `model.matrix(mpg ~ . - 1, data = cars)`. Removing the intercept *inside the formula* makes R code the **first** factor with **all** its levels (`cyl4`, `cyl6`, `cyl8`). If that matrix is later used in a model *with* an intercept, the three dummies add up to the intercept column — perfect collinearity — and `lm()` returns `NA` for one coefficient:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
X_bad <- model.matrix(mpg ~ . - 1, data = cars)
coef(lm(y ~ X_bad))[c("X_badcyl4", "X_badcyl6", "X_badcyl8")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> X_badcyl4 X_badcyl6 X_badcyl8 
#>    -1.637    -3.298        NA
```


:::
:::


Use `model.matrix(y ~ ., data)[, -1]` (one reference level per factor). The penalty would hide the problem in glmnet, but the coefficients of the three `cyl` dummies would no longer have a clear meaning.
:::

## 5. Ridge regression with glmnet

`glmnet()` fits the model for a whole sequence of 100 values of $\lambda$ at once. `alpha = 0` gives ridge.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_ridge <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0)
plot(fit_ridge, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Ridge coefficient paths for the mtcars model. Each line is one coefficient. On the right (large lambda) all coefficients are squeezed towards zero; moving left, the penalty weakens and they approach their OLS values. The numbers on top are the number of non-zero coefficients — always all of them for ridge.](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-ridge-path-1.png){#fig-ridge-path fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read a coefficient path

- The x axis is $\log(\lambda)$, increasing to the right. The **strongest** penalty is on the **right**, where all coefficients are close to 0; the weakest is on the left, close to OLS.
- The y axis shows each coefficient (on the original scale of its predictor); the number at the left end of each line is its column in `X` (1 = `cyl6`, 2 = `cyl8`, and so on).
- With ridge no line reaches 0 exactly before the far right; correlated predictors move together.
:::

Which $\lambda$ should we use? The one that predicts new data best — estimated by cross-validation.

## 6. Choosing $\lambda$ by cross-validation

`cv.glmnet()` runs $k$-fold cross-validation (10 folds by default) over the whole $\lambda$ sequence and records, for each $\lambda$, the mean CV error and its standard error.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(123)
cv_ridge <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0)
plot(cv_ridge)
c(lambda_min = cv_ridge$lambda.min, lambda_1se = cv_ridge$lambda.1se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> lambda_min lambda_1se 
#>      2.503      9.206
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-validated mean squared error of ridge regression as a function of log(lambda), with ±1 standard error bars. The two dotted lines mark lambda.min (left) and lambda.1se (right).](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-cv-ridge-1.png){#fig-cv-ridge fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Two values of $\lambda$ are reported:

- **`lambda.min`**: the $\lambda$ with the **lowest** mean CV error.
- **`lambda.1se`**: the **largest** $\lambda$ whose CV error is within **one standard error** of the minimum.

`lambda.1se` applies the **one-standard-error rule** from [Model selection](40-model-selection.qmd): differences in CV error smaller than their standard error are mostly noise, so among the models that are statistically indistinguishable from the best we choose the **most regularised** one. It has larger $\lambda$, therefore smaller coefficients and — for the lasso — fewer non-zero coefficients. It is the **more parsimonious and more stable** choice; `lambda.min` tends to keep more noise and changes more from one CV run to the next. `lambda.min` can be preferable when pure predictive accuracy matters more than simplicity and the sample is large.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cbind(min = coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.min")[, 1],
      `1se` = coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.1se")[, 1],
      ols = coef(m_ols)) |>
  round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                min    1se    ols
#> (Intercept) 19.383 17.905 17.820
#> cyl6        -1.285 -0.698 -1.660
#> cyl8        -0.822 -0.965  1.637
#> disp        -0.006 -0.006  0.014
#> hp          -0.014 -0.010 -0.046
#> drat         1.019  1.019  0.026
#> wt          -1.280 -0.891 -3.806
#> qsec         0.183  0.165  0.647
#> vs1          0.933  0.938  1.747
#> ammanual     1.674  1.210  2.617
#> gear         0.614  0.523  0.764
#> carb        -0.502 -0.373  0.509
```


:::
:::


Overall the coefficients at `lambda.1se` are pulled further towards zero than at `lambda.min`, and both sets are more moderate than OLS. Look at `cyl8`: OLS estimates 1.64 — eight-cylinder cars more economical than four-cylinder ones of the same weight and power, an artefact of collinearity — while ridge at `lambda.1se` gives -0.97.

We can mark the chosen $\lambda$ on the coefficient path. The path is drawn against $\log(\lambda)$, so the vertical line must be at **`log(lambda)`**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(fit_ridge, xvar = "lambda")
abline(v = log(cv_ridge$lambda.min), lty = 2)
abline(v = log(cv_ridge$lambda.1se), lty = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Ridge coefficient paths with lambda.min (dashed) and lambda.1se (dotted).](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-ridge-path-line-1.png){#fig-ridge-path-line fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


## 7. The lasso: shrinkage and selection

`alpha = 1` gives the lasso:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_lasso <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)
plot(fit_lasso, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Lasso coefficient paths. Moving from right (strong penalty) to left, predictors enter the model one at a time; the numbers on top count the non-zero coefficients.](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-lasso-path-1.png){#fig-lasso-path fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(123)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)
plot(cv_lasso)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-validated MSE of the lasso. The numbers on top are the number of non-zero coefficients at each lambda.](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-cv-lasso-1.png){#fig-cv-lasso fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
b_lasso <- cbind(min = coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min")[, 1],
                 `1se` = coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")[, 1])
round(b_lasso, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                min    1se
#> (Intercept) 25.905 32.006
#> cyl6        -1.642  0.000
#> cyl8         0.000  0.000
#> disp         0.000 -0.001
#> hp          -0.029 -0.020
#> drat         0.233  0.217
#> wt          -2.619 -2.982
#> qsec         0.232  0.000
#> vs1          1.062  0.145
#> ammanual     1.998  0.000
#> gear         0.250  0.000
#> carb         0.000  0.000
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
colSums(b_lasso[-1, ] != 0)    # non-zero coefficients (excluding intercept)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> min 1se 
#>   8   5
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- At `lambda.min` the lasso keeps 8 predictors; at `lambda.1se` only 5: disp, hp, drat, wt, vs1.
- A coefficient of exactly 0 (printed as `0`) means the predictor has been **dropped**.
- The surviving coefficients are **shrunk**: smaller in absolute value than they would be in an OLS fit with only those predictors.
- With strongly correlated predictors, *which* one the lasso keeps can be somewhat arbitrary: weight and displacement carry much the same information. Do not read the selection as "the other variables do not matter".
:::

Because cross-validation splits the data at random, `lambda.1se` and the selected set can change with the seed. Try a few seeds (Exercise 1): this is a reminder that selection from 32 observations is fragile.

## 8. Elastic net and an honest comparison with OLS

### Choosing $\alpha$

The elastic net has two tuning parameters. A simple approach is to run `cv.glmnet()` for a few values of $\alpha$ using the **same folds** (`foldid`), so that the comparison is not distorted by different random splits:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
foldid <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(X)))
alphas <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
cv_by_alpha <- lapply(alphas, \(a) cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = a,
                                             foldid = foldid))

tibble(
  alpha = alphas,
  rmse_min = sapply(cv_by_alpha, \(cv) sqrt(min(cv$cvm))),
  rmse_1se = sapply(cv_by_alpha,
                    \(cv) sqrt(cv$cvm[cv$lambda == cv$lambda.1se])),
  nonzero_1se = sapply(cv_by_alpha,
                       \(cv) cv$nzero[cv$lambda == cv$lambda.1se])
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   alpha rmse_min rmse_1se nonzero_1se
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>
#> 1  0       2.618    2.893          11
#> 2  0.25    2.712    2.978           8
#> 3  0.5     2.722    2.955           7
#> 4  0.75    2.710    2.939           7
#> 5  1       2.706    2.966           5
```


:::
:::


`cvm` is the mean CV **squared** error, so we take its square root to get an RMSE in mpg. With 32 cars, the differences between values of $\alpha$ are small compared with their uncertainty; what changes clearly is the number of predictors kept.

### Does penalization beat OLS here?

The old way to answer this — one train/test split with 8 test cars — gives an answer that depends mostly on *which* 8 cars were drawn ([Model selection](40-model-selection.qmd), Section 6). Instead we use **repeated 5-fold cross-validation**. Because `cv.glmnet()` itself uses cross-validation to choose $\lambda$, it must run **inside** each training fold (nested CV): the held-out fold must play no part in choosing $\lambda$.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rmse_vec <- function(y, y_hat) sqrt(mean((y - y_hat)^2))

set.seed(2026)
cv_compare <- replicate(10, {
  folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(X)))
  sapply(1:5, \(i) {
    train <- folds != i
    ols <- lm(mpg ~ ., data = cars[train, ])
    ridge <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0, nfolds = 5)
    lasso <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 1, nfolds = 5)
    c(ols   = rmse_vec(y[!train], predict(ols, cars[!train, ])),
      ridge = rmse_vec(y[!train], predict(ridge, newx = X[!train, ],
                                          s = "lambda.1se")),
      lasso = rmse_vec(y[!train], predict(lasso, newx = X[!train, ],
                                          s = "lambda.1se")))
  }) |>
    rowMeans()
})
cv_rmse <- rowMeans(cv_compare)
round(cv_rmse, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   ols ridge lasso 
#>  3.64  2.97  3.21
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
apply(cv_compare, 1, sd) |> round(2)    # variability across repeats
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   ols ridge lasso 
#>  0.55  0.11  0.19
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- Each number is the RMSE (in mpg) for cars **not used** to fit the model or to choose $\lambda$, averaged over 5 folds × 10 repetitions.
- OLS with all 11 coefficients: 3.64; ridge: 2.97; lasso: 3.21 mpg.
- The second line shows how much each estimate moves between repetitions — a reminder that differences of a few tenths of a mpg are within the noise for a dataset this small.
:::

The predictors' standardisation is recomputed by `glmnet()` within each training fold, and `model.matrix()` only applies a fixed coding, so nothing leaks from the held-out fold. The real strength of penalization shows when there are **many** predictors relative to the number of observations — the next section.

## 9. When $p > n$: lasso as a variable selector

With more predictors than observations, least squares has no unique solution. We simulate 50 observations of 200 predictors, of which only the first 5 truly affect $y$:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
p <- 200
X_sim <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n,
                dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:p)))
beta_true <- c(3, -2.5, 2, -1.5, 1, rep(0, p - 5))
y_sim <- drop(X_sim %*% beta_true + rnorm(n))

sum(is.na(coef(lm(y_sim ~ X_sim))))   # coefficients OLS cannot estimate
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 151
```


:::
:::


OLS can estimate at most 50 coefficients; 151 are returned as `NA`, and the 50 it does estimate fit the data perfectly (zero residuals) — useless for prediction. The lasso has no such problem:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2)
cv_sim <- cv.glmnet(X_sim, y_sim, alpha = 1)

selected <- function(cv, s) {
  b <- coef(cv, s = s)[-1, 1]
  names(b)[b != 0]
}
sel_min <- selected(cv_sim, "lambda.min")
sel_1se <- selected(cv_sim, "lambda.1se")
true_vars <- paste0("x", 1:5)

tibble(rule = c("lambda.min", "lambda.1se"),
       selected = c(length(sel_min), length(sel_1se)),
       true_found = c(sum(true_vars %in% sel_min),
                      sum(true_vars %in% sel_1se)),
       false_positives = c(sum(!sel_min %in% true_vars),
                           sum(!sel_1se %in% true_vars)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   rule       selected true_found false_positives
#>   <chr>         <int>      <int>           <int>
#> 1 lambda.min       24          5              19
#> 2 lambda.1se       13          5               8
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(j = 1:p,
       estimate = coef(cv_sim, s = "lambda.1se")[-1, 1],
       truth = beta_true) |>
  ggplot(aes(j, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = j <= 5)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth), shape = 4, size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "#D55E00"),
                      labels = c("noise", "true signal")) +
  labs(x = "Predictor index", y = "Coefficient", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Lasso estimates at lambda.1se for the 200 simulated predictors (points) and true coefficients (crosses). Almost all noise predictors are set exactly to zero; the true ones are found but shrunk towards zero.](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-pn-coefs-1.png){#fig-pn-coefs fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- At `lambda.1se` the lasso kept 13 of 200 predictors, including 5 of the 5 true ones and 8 noise variables.
- At `lambda.min` it kept 24: the true signals plus many more noise variables. The smaller penalty buys a slightly lower CV error at the price of a much less parsimonious model.
- The estimates of the true coefficients are **biased towards zero** (the crosses lie farther from 0 than the points). This is the price of the penalty. If clean coefficient estimates are needed, a common two-step approach is to refit OLS on the selected variables — but then the usual p-values are no longer valid (see the box below).
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Penalized regression is a prediction tool

`glmnet` reports no standard errors or p-values, and for good reason: the coefficients are deliberately biased, and the selection of variables was made with the same data. Running `lm()` on the variables selected by the lasso and reading its p-values has the same problem as stepwise selection ([Model selection](40-model-selection.qmd), Section 4). Valid post-selection inference requires special methods (for example the **selectiveInference** package) and is beyond this course. Use penalized models when the goal is **prediction**, or as an exploratory screen.
:::

## 10. The same with tidymodels

In the machine-learning lessons that follow, models are built with **tidymodels** ([The machine-learning workflow](../10-ml/44-ml-workflow.qmd)). The glmnet model is `linear_reg()` with two tuning parameters: `penalty` (= $\lambda$) and `mixture` (= $\alpha$).

**Recipe** — the preprocessing, estimated on the training data inside each resample:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cars_rec <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = cars) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>       # k - 1 dummies per factor
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())      # mean 0, SD 1
```
:::


`step_dummy()` creates $k - 1$ indicator columns per factor (the same coding as `model.matrix(...)[, -1]`), and `step_normalize()` standardises every predictor, including the dummies, so that the penalty treats them on a common scale.

**Model and workflow:**


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
enet_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

enet_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(cars_rec) |>
  add_model(enet_spec)
```
:::


**Resamples and grid.** With only 32 cars we use repeated 5-fold CV and skip a separate test set; with a larger dataset you would first set one aside with `initial_split()` and evaluate the final model on it once with `last_fit()`. (Stratifying the folds by a numeric outcome needs more observations than we have, so we do not use `strata` here.)


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
cars_folds <- vfold_cv(cars, v = 5, repeats = 5)

enet_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  penalty = 10^seq(-3, 1, length.out = 30),
  mixture = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
)

enet_res <- tune_grid(enet_wf, resamples = cars_folds, grid = enet_grid,
                      metrics = metric_set(rmse))
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
autoplot(enet_res)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-validated RMSE of the elastic net for each combination of penalty (x axis, log scale) and mixture (colour).](43-penalized-regression_files/figure-html/fig-tm-tune-1.png){#fig-tm-tune fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


**Choosing the parameters:**


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
show_best(enet_res, metric = "rmse", n = 5)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>   penalty mixture .metric .estimator  mean     n std_err .config          
#>     <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>            
#> 1   2.807       0 rmse    standard   2.515    25  0.1364 pre0_mod126_post0
#> 2   3.857       0 rmse    standard   2.524    25  0.1462 pre0_mod131_post0
#> 3   2.043       0 rmse    standard   2.527    25  0.1281 pre0_mod121_post0
#> 4   1.487       0 rmse    standard   2.553    25  0.1215 pre0_mod116_post0
#> 5   5.298       0 rmse    standard   2.560    25  0.1575 pre0_mod136_post0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
best_rmse <- select_best(enet_res, metric = "rmse")
best_1se <- select_by_one_std_err(enet_res, desc(penalty), metric = "rmse")
bind_rows(best = best_rmse, one_se = best_1se, .id = "rule")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   rule   penalty mixture .config          
#>   <chr>    <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>            
#> 1 best     2.807       0 pre0_mod126_post0
#> 2 one_se   7.279       0 pre0_mod141_post0
```


:::
:::


`select_best()` is the analogue of `lambda.min`. `select_by_one_std_err()` implements the one-standard-error rule: among the combinations whose mean RMSE is within one standard error of the best, it returns the **simplest**, where we define "simplest" by sorting on `desc(penalty)` — the largest penalty first. This is the analogue of `lambda.1se`.

**Final model** — refit on all the data with the chosen parameters:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
final_fit <- enet_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best_1se) |>
  fit(data = cars)

final_fit |>
  extract_fit_parsnip() |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(estimate != 0)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    term        estimate penalty
#>    <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)  20.09     7.279
#>  2 disp         -0.7135   7.279
#>  3 hp           -0.7409   7.279
#>  4 drat          0.5605   7.279
#>  5 wt           -0.9409   7.279
#>  6 qsec          0.3021   7.279
#>  7 gear          0.4024   7.279
#>  8 carb         -0.6507   7.279
#>  9 cyl_X6       -0.3421   7.279
#> 10 cyl_X8       -0.4880   7.279
#> 11 vs_X1         0.4814   7.279
#> 12 am_manual     0.6494   7.279
```


:::
:::


These coefficients are on the **standardised** scale (because of `step_normalize()`): each is the change in mpg for a one-standard-deviation change in the predictor, which makes their sizes directly comparable. The fitted workflow can be used with `predict(final_fit, new_data = ...)`, and the recipe is applied to new data automatically.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Calling `lambda.min` the parsimonious choice.** It is the other way round: `lambda.1se` has the *larger* penalty, the smaller coefficients and (for the lasso) fewer predictors.
2. **Drawing the chosen $\lambda$ in the wrong place.** `plot(fit, xvar = "lambda")` uses $\log(\lambda)$ on the x axis, so the line is `abline(v = log(cv$lambda.1se))`, not `-log(...)`.
3. **Including all levels of a factor plus an intercept** (`model.matrix(y ~ . - 1)`). Use `model.matrix(y ~ ., data)[, -1]` or `step_dummy()`.
4. **Not standardising** when you fit penalties outside glmnet (or turning off `standardize`). The penalty would then depend on the units of measurement.
5. **Judging the model on one tiny test set** or choosing $\lambda$ with the data used to evaluate it. Use (repeated, nested) cross-validation.
6. **Reading p-values after lasso selection**, or interpreting the lasso's choice among correlated predictors as evidence that the dropped ones are irrelevant.
:::

## 11. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What happens to the lasso coefficients as $\lambda \to 0$? And as $\lambda$ becomes very large?

As $\lambda \to 0$ the penalty vanishes and the coefficients approach the OLS estimates (when OLS exists). As $\lambda$ grows they shrink, one by one they become exactly 0, and for $\lambda$ large enough all of them are 0: the model predicts the mean of $y$ for everyone.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Why is `lambda.1se` usually larger than `lambda.min`?

By definition it is the **largest** $\lambda$ whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum. Moving from `lambda.min` towards larger penalties, the CV error rises slowly at first; `lambda.1se` is the furthest point before the increase exceeds one standard error.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. You have 10 strongly correlated predictors that all carry similar information. Ridge or lasso?

Ridge (or an elastic net with small $\alpha$) spreads the weight over the correlated group and is stable. The lasso tends to pick one or two of them somewhat arbitrarily, and which ones can change from sample to sample.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. Why must predictors be standardised before applying the penalty?

The penalty is a sum over coefficients, and a coefficient's size depends on its predictor's units. Without standardisation, a predictor measured in large units (small coefficient) is barely penalised, and one in small units is heavily penalised — for reasons that have nothing to do with the data.
:::

## 12. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — the lasso's choice is fragile.** Run `cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)` on the `mtcars` design matrix with five different seeds. For each run, record `lambda.1se` and the names of the predictors with non-zero coefficients at `lambda.1se`. Are the selected sets always the same?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
for (s in 1:5) {
  set.seed(s)
  cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)
  b <- coef(cv, s = "lambda.1se")[-1, 1]
  cat("seed", s, ": lambda.1se =", round(cv$lambda.1se, 2), "->",
      names(b)[b != 0], "\n")
}
```
With only 32 cars, `lambda.1se` moves noticeably from seed to seed, and so can the number of predictors kept: some predictors (weight, for instance) tend to survive in most runs, others come and go. A more stable choice can be obtained by averaging the CV curves over several runs (or using repeated CV, as in tidymodels), but the lesson is general: variable selection from small samples should be treated with caution.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — debug.** A student plots the lasso path and the chosen penalty with

```r
plot(fit_lasso, xvar = "lambda")
abline(v = -log(cv_lasso$lambda.min), col = "red")
```

and writes: *"I use `lambda.min` because it gives the most parsimonious model."* Find the two errors.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
1. The x axis is $\log(\lambda)$, so the line must be at `log(cv_lasso$lambda.min)`. Because $\lambda < 1$ here, $\log(\lambda)$ is negative and $-\log(\lambda)$ is positive: the red line ends up on the wrong side of the plot, at a value of $\lambda$ that was never chosen.
2. `lambda.min` is the **least** regularised of the two standard choices. The parsimonious one is `lambda.1se`.

```r
plot(fit_lasso, xvar = "lambda")
abline(v = log(cv_lasso$lambda.1se), col = "red")
```
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — predict the output.** Weight `wt` is in thousands of pounds. Suppose you create `X_lb` by multiplying the `wt` column by 1000 (weight in pounds) and refit the lasso. What happens to the coefficient of weight (a) with the default `standardize = TRUE`, (b) with `standardize = FALSE`? Check with `glmnet(..., lambda = cv_lasso$lambda.1se)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) With standardisation, the fit is the same model: the weight coefficient is simply divided by 1000 and all other coefficients are unchanged. (b) Without it, the coefficient of weight in pounds is tiny, so penalising it costs almost nothing: the lasso keeps weight more easily and the balance with the other predictors changes. The result depends on an arbitrary choice of units — which is why glmnet standardises by default.

```r
X_lb <- X
X_lb[, "wt"] <- X_lb[, "wt"] * 1000
lam <- cv_lasso$lambda.1se
cbind(original = coef(glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lam))[, 1],
      std_true = coef(glmnet(X_lb, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lam))[, 1],
      std_false = coef(glmnet(X_lb, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lam,
                              standardize = FALSE))[, 1]) |>
  round(4)
```
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — interpret an output.** A `cv.glmnet()` lasso fit reports: `lambda.min` = 0.08 with 9 non-zero coefficients and CV MSE 7.1; `lambda.1se` = 0.90 with 3 non-zero coefficients and CV MSE 8.0; the standard error of the CV error at `lambda.min` is 1.3. Which model would you report and why? What would change your mind?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The difference in CV MSE (8.0 − 7.1 = 0.9) is smaller than one standard error (1.3): the data cannot really distinguish the two models. The 3-predictor model at `lambda.1se` is simpler, easier to explain, and its selection is more likely to be reproducible, so it is the natural choice. If small gains in accuracy were valuable (and confirmed on a large test set), or if many repeated CV runs consistently favoured the larger model, `lambda.min` could be justified.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — mini-analysis: how reliable is lasso selection?** Repeat the $p > n$ simulation of Section 9 twenty times (new `X_sim`, `y_sim` and CV folds each time). For each run, record the number of true predictors found and the number of false positives at `lambda.min` and at `lambda.1se`. Summarise the averages.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
set.seed(10)
runs <- replicate(20, {
  Xs <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n,
               dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:p)))
  ys <- drop(Xs %*% beta_true + rnorm(n))
  cv <- cv.glmnet(Xs, ys, alpha = 1)
  s_min <- selected(cv, "lambda.min")
  s_1se <- selected(cv, "lambda.1se")
  c(true_min = sum(true_vars %in% s_min),
    false_min = sum(!s_min %in% true_vars),
    true_1se = sum(true_vars %in% s_1se),
    false_1se = sum(!s_1se %in% true_vars))
})
rowMeans(runs)
```
Typically both rules find all or almost all of the 5 true predictors (the weakest, with coefficient 1, is the one most often missed), but `lambda.min` also lets in many more noise variables than `lambda.1se`. For **variable selection**, `lambda.1se` is clearly the better rule; neither rule is perfect, and the exact counts vary from run to run.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 6 — bias and variance across $\lambda$.** Using `ridge_coef()` and the simulation of Section 2 (1000 datasets for each value), compute the bias, variance and MSE of $\hat\beta_1$ for $\lambda$ = 0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 2 and 10. Describe the pattern.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
set.seed(2026)
lambdas <- c(0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 2, 10)
bv <- sapply(lambdas, \(l) {
  b1 <- replicate(1000, {
    x1 <- rnorm(30)
    x2 <- 0.95 * x1 + sqrt(1 - 0.95^2) * rnorm(30)
    y <- x1 + x2 + rnorm(30, sd = 2)
    ridge_coef(cbind(x1, x2), y, l)[1]
  })
  c(lambda = l, bias = mean(b1) - 1, variance = var(b1),
    mse = mean((b1 - 1)^2))
})
round(t(bv), 3)
```
As $\lambda$ grows the **variance** falls steadily (from about 1.5 at $\lambda = 0$ to almost 0), while the **bias** grows in magnitude (from about 0 to about −0.84 at $\lambda = 10$). The **MSE** first drops sharply, reaches its minimum around $\lambda = 0.5$ (about 0.08), then rises again as the bias dominates (about 0.7 at $\lambda = 10$). This U-shape is the bias–variance trade-off; cross-validation is a way to find the bottom of the U without knowing the truth.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `model.matrix(y ~ ., data)[, -1]` | numeric design matrix with $k-1$ dummies per factor |
| `glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0 / 1 / 0.5)` | ridge / lasso / elastic net path over many $\lambda$ |
| `plot(fit, xvar = "lambda")`, `abline(v = log(lambda))` | coefficient paths against $\log\lambda$ |
| `cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha, foldid = )` | CV error over the $\lambda$ path |
| `lambda.min`, `lambda.1se` | best CV error; most regularised within 1 SE (simpler, more stable) |
| `coef(cv, s = "lambda.1se")`, `predict(cv, newx, s = )` | coefficients and predictions at a chosen $\lambda$ |
| `linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) \|> set_engine("glmnet")` | the same model in tidymodels |
| `step_dummy()`, `step_normalize()` | dummy coding and standardisation inside a recipe |
| `tune_grid()`, `select_best()`, `select_by_one_std_err(..., desc(penalty))` | tuning and the one-standard-error rule |

- Penalization **shrinks** coefficients, trading a little bias for a large reduction in variance.
- **Ridge** keeps all predictors; the **lasso** sets some exactly to zero; the **elastic net** mixes the two.
- **Standardise** predictors so that the penalty does not depend on units (glmnet does it by default).
- Choose $\lambda$ by cross-validation; **`lambda.1se`** is the parsimonious, stable choice.
- Evaluate with **repeated, nested** CV, and treat penalized models as **prediction** tools, not sources of p-values.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
